title: Proximity Matters: Local Proximity Enhanced Balancing for Treatment Effect Estimation

problem.claim: Estimating heterogeneous treatment effects from observational data is challenged by treatment selection bias.

gap.claim: Existing latent-space balancing methods focus on global alignment and often overlook local proximity among similar units.

contributions.claim: The study proposes Proximity-enhanced CounterFactual Regression (CFR-Pro) to use local proximity for representation balancing in heterogeneous treatment effect estimation.
CFR-Pro introduces a pair-wise proximity regularizer based on optimal transport for incorporating local proximity into discrepancy calculation.
The study develops an informative subspace projector that trades off distance precision for improved sample complexity under high dimensionality and limited data.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that extensive experiments show CFR-Pro accurately matches units across treatment groups, mitigates treatment selection bias, and outperforms competitors.
The authors report that implementation code is available.

narrative_sequence.summary: Observational heterogeneous treatment effect estimation faces treatment selection bias.
Existing methods globally align treatment groups in latent space, while local proximity is often overlooked.
CFR-Pro uses an optimal-transport pair-wise proximity regularizer and an informative subspace projector to improve proximity-aware balancing under dimensionality and data limitations.
The authors report improved matching, bias mitigation, and performance relative to competitors, with code availability.

source_observation.claim: Global representation alignment may overlook useful local similarity structure among units.

interpretation.claim: Balancing methods may benefit from incorporating neighborhood-level relationships in addition to global distribution matching.

application.claim: For observational treatment effect estimation, consider proximity-aware regularization when similar units are expected to have similar outcomes.

exception.claim: High dimensionality and limited data may make proximity and discrepancy estimates ineffective without dimensionality management.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify datasets, sample sizes, treatment settings, or evaluation metrics.
The abstract does not provide quantitative performance results or details of the competing methods.
